text: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API) is the official compendium of quality standards for Ayurvedic drugs. Published by Ministry of AYUSH. Contents: monographs for single drugs (herbs, minerals) and formulations — description, identification tests, purity standards, assay methods, storage, therapeutic use. Currently 8 volumes (single drugs) + formulation volumes. Compliance: ASU drugs must meet API standards for licensing. For AYUSH manufacturers: API is your quality benchmark; ensure raw materials and products meet specified parameters.

Key standardization parameters for AYUSH products: 1) Identity — correct species, authentic material (macroscopy, microscopy, TLC fingerprint). 2) Purity — absence of adulterants, heavy metals within limits (Pb<10ppm, As<3ppm, Hg<1ppm, Cd<0.3ppm), microbial limits, pesticide residues. 3) Potency — marker compound content (curcumin in turmeric, withanolides in ashwagandha). 4) Stability — shelf life, storage conditions. For IP: standardization creates differentiable products; proprietary standardization methods can be protected.

Marker compounds are characteristic chemicals used to standardize herbal products. Examples: Curcuminoids in Curcuma longa, Withanolides in Withania somnifera, Bacosides in Bacopa monnieri, Andrographolide in Andrographis paniculata, Piperine in Piper nigrum. Analytical methods: HPLC, HPTLC, UV-Vis spectrophotometry. API specifies marker requirements where available. For IP: developing validated analytical methods for markers can be published/patented; proprietary marker profiles differentiate products.

Heavy metals in AYUSH products are a major quality and safety concern. Sources: contaminated raw materials (soil, water pollution), processing equipment, mineral-based preparations (Bhasmas). Regulatory limits (CDSCO): Lead 10 ppm, Arsenic 3 ppm, Mercury 1 ppm, Cadmium 0.3 ppm. For Bhasmas: specific limits may differ due to intentional mineral content. Testing: AAS, ICP-OES, ICP-MS methods. For AYUSH: test every batch, reject non-compliant materials, document testing. Heavy metal issues cause recalls and market access problems.

Microbial quality standards for AYUSH products: Total aerobic microbial count (TAMC) — typically <10^5 CFU/g for oral products. Total yeast and mold count (TYMC) — typically <10^3 CFU/g. Specific pathogens: E. coli (absent), Salmonella (absent in 10g), S. aureus (absent). For products administered other routes: stricter limits apply. For Bhasmas: may be sterile or near-sterile due to high-temperature processing. Testing: standard plate count methods, specific pathogen tests. For AYUSH: implement GMP to control microbial quality.

Stability testing establishes shelf life under specified storage conditions. ICH-like guidelines adapted for AYUSH: Accelerated stability: 40°C±2°C / 75%RH±5% for 6 months. Long-term stability: 30°C±2°C / 65%RH±5% for 12-24 months. Real-time stability: actual storage conditions over shelf-life period. Testing points: 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, 24 months. Parameters: physical characteristics, assay, degradation products, microbial quality. For AYUSH: stability data required for new product registration; supports shelf-life claims and IP.

Schedule T of Drugs and Cosmetics Rules specifies GMP for ASU drugs. Key requirements: 1) Premises — adequate space, cleanliness, pest control. 2) Equipment — suitable, maintained, calibrated. 3) Personnel — trained, qualified, hygiene. 4) Materials — authenticated, tested, properly stored. 5) Documentation — batch records, SOPs, specifications. 6) Production — validated processes, in-process controls. 7) Quality control — testing, release procedures. 8) Self-inspection — regular audits. For IP: GMP processes can include proprietary elements; GMP compliance is prerequisite for commercializing patented products.

Raw material authentication ensures correct identity: 1) Organoleptic evaluation — appearance, odor, taste, texture. 2) Macroscopy — gross anatomical features. 3) Microscopy — cellular structures, diagnostic elements. 4) Chemical tests — specific reactions for identification. 5) TLC/HPTLC fingerprinting — chromatographic profile matching. 6) DNA barcoding — genetic identification (emerging). Reference materials: compare with authenticated voucher specimens. For AYUSH: document authentication for every batch; adulteration with cheaper substitutes is common problem.

NABL (National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories) accreditation ensures testing quality. Accredited labs: demonstrate competence, follow ISO 17025 standards, undergo periodic audits. For regulatory submissions: NABL-accredited lab reports often required. List of accredited labs available on nabl-india.org. For AYUSH: use NABL-accredited labs for critical testing (heavy metals, microbial, assay). In-house labs can seek NABL accreditation for credibility. Third-party testing adds independence to quality claims.

Reference standards are authenticated samples used for comparison in testing. Sources: Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission (IPC), CSIR-IIIM (Jammu), NISCAIR, commercial suppliers (Sigma-Aldrich, LGC). Types: Primary standards (highest purity, certified), Secondary/working standards (calibrated against primary). For AYUSH: use authenticated reference standards for marker compound analysis. Store properly, verify identity, track lot numbers. Reference standard costs add to testing expense but ensure reliability.

Quality certifications for AYUSH products: 1) ISO 9001 — quality management system. 2) ISO 22000/FSSC 22000 — food safety (for FSSAI-regulated products). 3) WHO-GMP — pharmaceutical manufacturing. 4) HACCP — hazard analysis and critical control points. 5) GMP-ASU — Schedule T compliance. 6) Organic certification — NPOP/PGS India. 7) Halal certification — for Middle East export. Multiple certifications demonstrate commitment to quality. For AYUSH: select certifications based on target markets and product types.

Quality by Design (QbD) approach for AYUSH: 1) Define Target Product Quality Profile — what quality attributes matter. 2) Identify Critical Quality Attributes — parameters affecting safety/efficacy. 3) Identify Critical Material Attributes — raw material factors. 4) Identify Critical Process Parameters — process variables affecting quality. 5) Develop Design Space — proven acceptable ranges. 6) Implement Control Strategy — ongoing quality assurance. QbD shifts from testing-for-quality to building-in-quality. For AYUSH IP: QbD documentation supports patent claims for process improvements.
